\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Under fixed temperature $\tau$ and nucleus $p$, iterative conditioning shifts the input distribution's location (mean NLL decreases as text becomes more predictable), but shape parameters (variance, tail behavior) are anchored by the fixed sampling regime.
Sampling ablation supports this ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$: ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation; $t = 1.0$: $-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
DDR is a parameter-dependent phenomenon (modulated by temperature and prompt type), not an intrinsic property of recursive generation.
Entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.17$) occupies an intermediate position between the drifting features ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and the near-stationary tail decay ($|\rho| = 0.04$).
Semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling).
The primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+: 86\% of binary errors are false negatives, with depth-2 error rate 48\% vs.\ 20\% for depth-4 (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
This asymmetry follows from DDR: the first recursive step produces the smallest location shift; larger generators exacerbate the overlap.
Cross-reference experiments confirm limited reference-family bias (F1 within 0.013\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow$ mismatch: F1 from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.

Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs, losing distributional coverage through parameter updates.
DDR operates in a different regime: inference-chain drift occurs with fixed parameters, is fully reversible, and affects shape features an order of magnitude less than central-tendency features.
Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA fine-tuning recovers F1\,=\,0.905 (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), evidence that richer signal exists beyond summary statistics.

Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base); this justifies our restriction to base models.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Under fixed temperature $\tau$ and nucleus $p$, iterative conditioning shifts the input distribution's location (mean NLL decreases as text becomes more predictable), but shape parameters (variance, tail behavior) are anchored by the fixed sampling regime.
Sampling ablation supports this ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$: ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation; $t = 1.0$: $-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
DDR is a parameter-dependent phenomenon (modulated by temperature and prompt type), not an intrinsic property of recursive generation.
Entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.17$) occupies an intermediate position between the drifting features ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and the near-stationary tail decay ($|\rho| = 0.04$).
Semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+ (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}), consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step.
Cross-reference experiments confirm limited reference-family bias (F1 within 0.013\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow$ mismatch: F1 from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.

Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; DDR operates in a different regime with fixed parameters, where inference-chain drift is fully reversible and affects shape features an order of magnitude less.
Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA recovers F1\,=\,0.905 (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming richer signal beyond summary statistics.
Instruction-tuned models show weaker fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base), justifying the base-model restriction.

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Recursive LLM generation chains, in which model outputs seed further generation, produce text with progressively altered distributional properties.
Understanding the structure of this drift is important for characterizing recursive generation dynamics, yet existing detection methods provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions without depth awareness.
We study eight base (pretrained) models from five families under standard decoding and identify a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): central-tendency features (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drift monotonically with generation depth, while shape features (entropy max, vocabulary tail slope) show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size, consistent with a location shift in the token-level negative log-likelihood distribution.
Framing depth estimation as coarse ordinal classification (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), a 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains (3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809) and binary F1\,=\,0.694 (95\% CI [.688, .700]) under leave-one-generator-out evaluation across eight generators, at substantially lower computational cost than multi-detector alternatives.
Equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\% margin, $p < 0.001$) confirms that depth-aware data selection yields training utility equivalent to random subsampling: the detected distributional shift does not translate to downstream perplexity degradation within $\leq$4 generations.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When the output of a language model is fed back as input to another (or the same) model, the resulting generation chain defines a discrete dynamical system over text distributions.
How do the distributional properties of generated text evolve across successive steps of this recursion?
The question is both theoretically fundamental and practically urgent: recursive chains are pervasive, with estimates suggesting 7--17\% of recent scientific papers contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and model outputs increasingly re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb}, with implications for data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} and corpus governance.
Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by coarse ordinal depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure the distributional dynamics of recursive generation; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation producing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution; one hypothesis is that the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.

The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains (3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809) and binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, outperforming all individual detection baselines by 6--11\,pp in 3-class F1, while multi-detector ensembles achieve slightly higher 3-class performance (0.795 vs.\ 0.774) at 2.4$\times$ the computational cost.
The signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Our contributions are threefold:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary real-vs-synthetic detection to classify text by coarse ordinal depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and construct an evaluation suite of 37K texts from eight base-model generators spanning five families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We identify \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): recursive generation is consistent with monotonic drift in central-tendency features ($|\rho| > 0.60$) while shape features show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect ($|\rho| < 0.10$). A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this structure achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains with a single 410M reference model.
    \item Via equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$), we show that depth-aware data selection yields training utility equivalent to random subsampling at equal sample count: the distributional shift DDR captures does not translate to downstream quality degradation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot reference-model approaches \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers \cite{ghostbuster,feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work pursues diverse signals including intrinsic dimensionality \cite{intrinsic_dimension}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, and distributional gap measures \cite{generator_barrier}; see \citet{wu_survey_2025} and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
A persistent limitation is that these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Recent multi-class extensions (role recognition in human-LLM collaboration \cite{beyond_binary}, multi-generator attribution \cite{semeval2024_task8}) discriminate among different \emph{sources} rather than recursive generation \emph{depth}.
Even when detection scores correlate with depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
Adversarial training approaches (e.g., RADAR \cite{radar}) improve robustness to paraphrasing but remain binary detectors without depth awareness.
Our contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (generation depth classification, framed within the broader ordinal classification literature \cite{gutierrez_ordinal_survey,coral_ordinal}) and the finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
This is orthogonal to source attribution \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}, which identifies \emph{which} model generated text; our LOGO evaluation decouples generator identity from depth.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad}, and model collapse is inevitable without fresh human data \cite{curse_of_recursion}, though careful data mixing can mitigate this \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation; our setting studies \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.
Iterative self-refinement \cite{self_refine} represents another form of recursive LLM processing, but targets output improvement through feedback loops rather than open-ended continuation; the distributional drift we study arises specifically from unconstrained recursive generation.

Two concurrent works are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss.
\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes; their analysis focuses on characterizing convergence behavior through model-based perplexity tracking.
We differ in three respects: (i) we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal; (ii) we use handcrafted features rather than model-internal representations, enabling the DDR decomposition into drifting vs.\ stationary components; and (iii) we focus on \emph{classifying} depth from text rather than characterizing the convergence dynamics of the generation process.

That both works independently converge on approximately three distinguishable classes reflects different mechanisms reaching the same practical ceiling.
\citet{markovian_chains} derive this bound from Markovian attractor dynamics: semantic-preservation constraints create fixed points where successive outputs become indistinguishable under model-internal perplexity.
